name: Magic Shave

lead: Magic Shave is a brand of chemical depilatory powder. Depilatories remove hair at the skin surface rather than destroying the follicle, so hair grows back.

It appears in the medical literature mainly through case reports of harm: a 1989 mass eye-injury incident aboard a ship and a 2000 case of poisoning after a product containing barium sulfide was swallowed.

paras: Chemical depilatories break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin so hair can be wiped away; they do not destroy the dermal papilla, so regrowth occurs. Wikipedia lists Magic Shave among powder-form depilatories.

A 1989 report described corneal alkali burns in 40 sailors from a powder suspected to be Magic Shave (calcium hydroxide). A 2000 case report described respiratory arrest and dangerous potassium disturbances after a man swallowed a barium sulfide depilatory of this brand.

lead: Magic Shave is a brand of chemical depilatory powder. Wikipedia lists it, alongside Nair and Veet, among depilatory products sold as gels, creams, lotions, aerosols, roll-ons and powders. [1]

Depilatories break down the keratin in hair so it can be wiped off; because they leave the dermal papilla intact, hair grows back. [1] The brand appears in the medical literature primarily in case reports of harm. [2][3]
infobox: Calcium hydroxide (1989 report) [3]; barium sulfide (2000 case report) [2]

paras: Typical depilatories use thioglycolic acid salts at high pH (around 12, kept by calcium or strontium hydroxide) to break disulfide bonds in keratin, with hair breakdown taking about 10 minutes. [1] Older sulfide ingredients such as strontium sulfide were largely replaced by thiols because of odour. [1]

No studies found of efficacy. The medical literature consists of case reports. A 2000 case described a 25-year-old man who ingested a barium sulfide depilatory (Magic Shave) and presented with muscle weakness, respiratory arrest, rhabdomyolysis and life-threatening hyperkalemia. [2] A 1989 report described 40 sailors who received eye injuries during a shipboard ceremony from a chemical agent suspected to be Magic Shave, a powder with calcium hydroxide; the corneal burns were alkali in nature, and 20 patients were admitted to sick bay for one to two days. [3]
Documented harms in the literature are ingestion poisoning [2] and alkali corneal burns from eye exposure. [3] Product-specific formulations may have changed since these reports.
